There's a legitimate case for SaaS being a bad industry in a world of AI, i get it, i use the tools, i've always thought hyperscalers had better businesses, with similar growth and actual earnings.

i know how to program. at least some amount of fear is valid for legacy SaaS (increased competition and lower margins seems like the most valid bear argument to me, as opposed to  ASI generating CRM tools for everyone). I can think of lots of counter arguments, but i will save it for another time.

That said, it is undeniable there was irrational fear and factor rotation in the market today.

You can see this because Feb 3 Oslo time, $OPRA put out this earnings release (attached), which was a solid beat and raise. The stock went vertical, going from 12.5 to 14.6, +17%.

$OPRA is a tricky company (do we really need another browser?), though it sells for a very discounted price and the numbers usually impress (2x sales, 10-12ish FCF/earnings yield, with 26% rev growth, while also paying a 6% dividend - representative of very solid execution).

The thing is, literally nothing changed between Feb 3 Oslo time, and Feb 3 US time. But the stock still tanked 8% today.

Whatever your view on Claude Code, in that 8 hours, nothing happened. $OPRA killed it on earnings, the stock went up a lot, then everyone got scared for no new reason, and it went down a lot.

That's how you know for sure there is irrational fear and automated trading mixed in with any valid criticisms people might come up with.

Most stuff I have done has gone extremely well (especially some space purchases early in the year, as well as $GOOG and $INTC which I trimmed a bit), but I went heavy into software (>27% of net equity in just application software at one point) on the drawdown, and it appears there was further to go. My view is we have mostly bottomed, but big losses in $DUOL and $DOCU, which I bought at what i consider very reasonable prices, as well as a major drawdown in an old $GENI position (which I have now dumped) stung a bit (all -30% and large positions). $GENI has nothing to do with the SaaS narrative, and I actually expect it to be ok, but still dumped that one as it is just not in line with where my head is at right now and the spot has only got more complicated with the companies latest move into the advertising space (perhaps a defensive positioning to get Kalshi to pay up for first party data?).

This did also contribute partially to my decision to sell a long time holding in $STZ. I still fully believe in the long term $STZ hold, but i sold it to upsize $GTLB and $SKM, which are directly related to the AI agents theme that I am spending a tonne of time thinking about and believe I can maybe generate a bit more alpha investing in.

I do still see some spots in SaaS that give me pause. For example, I think Cybersecurity is really important in the world of AI agents, but I still can't bring myself to buy $RBRK here at 10x rev. I should be desperate to buy everything right now if its a software bottom and I feel that software will be ok in the end... and yet... would really be hoping for something more like 6x rev on that. We shall see.

2. Drove the leverage a little bit cos somehow i am now a telco magnet.
Relative to my overall vague goal of remaining around 185% gross 85% net i've pushed things a bit. My reasoning is that a) i want to have yen debt against my CS Lumber position which is low vol and fairly safe (.5 p/tbv, all rental real estate).

b) somehow I have ended up with a bunch of Telcos as my top positions. These are all low PE, somewhat safe, fairly diversified companies, with a little torque on the AI theme. So I think staying 100% long despite the high gross leverage is ok.

An example is $SKM, who owns a bunch of Anthropic stock (estimates range from 1.7 billion to ~3 billion) but as far as I can tell, no one has nailed down the exact number. I'm a buyer of Anthropic at 350b market cap (not really, but if I could buy a 5% position at that price with no fees I would). So this is probably worth at least 20% of SKMs market cap.

But without making the position mega huge, it's really not going to have a big enough effect on my returns. However, given that SKM's telco branch should be fairly stable long term, I think running the position fairly big should be ok.

On top of this, SKM is also building out AI data centers - this is an extremely good sign because it means they are on top of the trend - they bought Anthropic shares early, they are building data centers... do you think they won't automate literally every part of their business that can be? SK Telecom has 24,000 employees. A tonne probably work in areas that can be automated or improved - obviously a huge amount of these employees are in things like customer success. But perhaps just as important, you just aren't getting the best programmers in the world at a telco. These merely 'decent' programmers are going to find that they are suddenly getting a lot more done. A dream scenarios is that all these employees need new jobs, and SKM is able to take the best ones and put them into adjacent markets with the help of AI. Not that crazy imo.

This is also part of my $VEON long thesis (and to a lesser extent Rakuten), this idea that foreign tech companies will be major AI beneficiaries because they are not as good at coding as US google employees.

In the US, February 7, 2026, there is an expectation that code will be generated much faster with AI, and be ALMOST as good as the best programmers code, but not quite. The rough edges will be polished off in code reviews, but there will still be some 'cruft' that develops over time. But in a developing country, the AI code is going to raise the overall code quality in most codebases significantly. This seems very good if you are the sort of industry where your strong market positioning will not be significantly impacted by other people also having good programmers.

The consumer: We saw interesting results out of $AFRM and it sold down. This was a curious data point and maybe a little worrying for my $DAVE / $KLAR positions. But my worries were alleviated quite quickly as $DAVE reported early and absolutely crushed their numbers. i bought more. You are paying 8x RR aEBITDA (just 4x the last quarter, so not even counting future growth). People say 8x is cheap for $PYPL w 4% growth, LOL. But instead of getting eifel towered by $KLAR/$AFRM on one side and Zelle on the other, you get >60% rev growth and >100% earnings growth and clear operating leverage. Who knows if this will continue but i've been saying that for at least a year now and the growth just keeps accelerating, not decaying.

$KLAR, I don't know what will happen. It was made extremely clear on $AFRM's last earnings call that $KLAR took $WMT as a customer from them, which would be an amazingly good sign.

But $AFRM also services $AMZN. I could see $WMT telling $AFRM it was us or them the second there was a viable BNPL alternative, so it doesn't necessarily mean $KLAR is massively outexecuting $AFRM. But it's still only good.

Seeing a pretty big mean reversion into software today although it looks like it's faded a bit. I continue to play both sides with positions in semis and also positions in software. Essentially, i am price sensitive and think disruption is here but the timelines people are projecting are just way too fast. The market is acting like incumbents are just going to roll over and die, like they have no moves to make. It would be prudent to spend more time studying Nexstar Media ( $NXST) and a little less time worrying.

Portfolio looks ok going into earnings for $DUOL. Since management already gave us bookings guidance, I don't think there should be as much vol as implied by options pricing, but, what do I know. Still like the spot a lot but i have an 18 month view here, not one earnings (especially not one we already guided w/ bookings).

The market says the big thing will be whether or not we hit earnings per share, but actually the more important angle is user growth since that's what management has said they are focused on. This isn't some trick, if you understand the app you legitimately can see that its a delicate balance between user growth/retention and monetization. This is essentially the YouTube model, where it is all about finding the optimal balance between saturating your free users with ads to maximize profitability and drive users to subscription, and optimizing retention / user growth.

I've been tracking the app store position for $DUOL the last few months and think user growth is pretty solid, I think we are consistently hitting at least 300,000 downloads per day for >100m downloads a year. Typically we sit around rank #32-38 in the apple app store Free category. This is pretty high for a 5b market cap company. In theory, we should get multiple drivers - higher conversion of downloads to DAU, uptake of the increasingly necessary MAX tier, and better monetization of the ad tier.

GL to anyone who is long the Green Bird 🫡

Might be cope but i think $DUOL still looks great, not financial advice / you will have to make up your own mind.

Obviously not a great guide but if you listen to @LuisvonAhn talk, it is very clear he is just playing the hand he was dealt optimally, but that there are some complexities balancing user growth against monetization. Every company has this issue. Look at the Trustpilot reviews for YouTube! 1.5 stars! And the same complaints about balancing the ad load against the subscriber base and some small segment of luddites complaining about AI.

Lets talk about the strategy, what I like, and what I don't.
1. Giving non-MAX callers access to AI video chat - this is essential.

I use Duolingo to learn Korean and frankly the video chat and touchless audio cards are like, 80% of the product now (the other 20% is the nice animations that make you addicted). It is the key narrative destroyer when people say Duolingo is not good for learning.

I would go further - just kill the MAX tier completely and give all SUPER subscribers unlimited video chat. Be aggresive, Learna is growing. We are way ahead still but just KO blow immediately. No quarter for enemies of the owl.

2. Acknowledging lower margins - but shoudl be more aggressive
This is obviously going to hurt earnings short term but its really not that bad. The market dgaf about earnings.

If we have 100m MAU and can get 30% of them to pay $6 a month (feels pretty reasonable if we significantly improve the product)
-180m rev per month
-2.16b rev per year.

Send EBITDA margin to 0% to get there, who cares. Just win, token cost going way down. Market will significantly prefer this much revenue growth with no earnings over where we are now.

If rev grows to 2b a year from here rapidly, market will apply a 5x rev multiple for sure for 10b market cap. Then stock based comp will be much cheaper, so we will get back the money anyway.

3. Just kill the music app, man
As a serious musician, the Duolingo music learning app is borderline offensive. It's fine, we all got excited branching out into new areas, Chess, Math, Music, etc. Everyone loves music! 2/3 worked! That's great.

But music won't, and buying this was a mistake. I use https://t.co/CKJDWatmaB's app for Chess sometimes, its great but Duolingo can compete here. My wife is 1800 rated at Chess, she says people are always telling her the Duolingo chess app is surprisingly good!

The math product obviously works and getting into schools will give us a higher retention product (dare i say Cradle to Grave?). And language learning with video tutors, also a great product. Keep all the best employees from this product and move them onto Chess or Math, get rid of the rest, and use the cost savings to be more aggressive with the SUPER plan.

Learning music on a phone is just never going to work, I wish it would. As a serious pianist as a kid and then later touring in a band, i constantly tried to figure out ways to improve at music while using a phone - the best thing you can do? Just listen to music. Also way more enjoyable. The music product is antithetical to Duolingo's mission.

Anyway, unfortunately this is going to be an 18 month story from here. Pod shops are not going to enjoy waiting, so i don't see us hitting $200 a share in 2026. But long term, I continue to believe Duolingo works and that the core narratives are all invalid

1. It is not Chegg.
2. Competitors cannot easily vibe code an alternative.
3. You can actually learn extremely effectively with the app because of the new Lily/Falstaff product.
